paragraphs: SELECT Name, Price chooses the two columns to display. We need the product name as well as its price so we can identify each item in the sorted result.

lines.title: Read every product
paragraphs: FROM Products tells SQL where to read the names and prices. We want every product, so we do not need a WHERE rule to leave any products out.
lines.watchOut: Choosing which rows to include and sorting those rows are different jobs.

question.prompt: Why is there no WHERE rule in this query?

choices.text: WHERE would delete the table.
choices.feedback: WHERE checks which rows to keep in a result; it does not delete the table.

choices.text: We want to include every product.
choices.feedback: Correct. We are changing their display order, not leaving any products out.

choices.text: FROM already sorts the prices.
choices.feedback: FROM names the table. ORDER BY is needed to choose the order.

prediction.prompt: All products are included. How can we make the cheapest appear first?

choices.feedback: Choosing columns does not sort prices.

choices.text: Keep only products costing more than 10.

choices.text: Sort by Price from the smallest value to the largest.
choices.feedback: Correct. Ascending order means smallest first and largest last.

lines.title: Sort from the lowest price to the highest
paragraphs: ORDER BY Price sorts the result using the numbers in the Price column. ASC means ascending: smaller numbers come before larger numbers.
The prices are shown as 3, 8, 12.50, 15, 18 and 24. Cable therefore appears first and Keyboard appears last. Sorting the result does not change the prices stored in the table.
lines.watchOut: ASC means smallest to largest. DESC means largest to smallest, so it would answer a different question.

choices.text: Mouse, because it was stored first.
choices.feedback: ORDER BY chooses a new display order using Price, not the original row position.

choices.text: Cable, because it costs 3.

lines.title: Check whether each name starts with A
paragraphs: LIKE checks text against a pattern. In 'A%', A must be at the start, and % allows zero or more characters after it. The whole pattern uses quotation marks because it is text.

Ada, Amir and Aisha appear. Ben starts with B, Hana starts with H and Cleo starts with C, so they are left out. A name that was just A would also match because % does not require any extra characters.
lines.watchOut: Name = 'A' would keep only the exact name A. LIKE 'A%' also allows Ada and Amir. '%A' would look for an A at the end instead.
